The New York Stock Exchange is a big building in New Jersey where computers trade stocks with each other. In this it is like all other modern U.S. stock exchanges, which are also big buildings in New Jersey where computers trade stocks with each other.[1] But unlike the other exchanges, NYSE is a data center with a keen sense of its history. There are six buttonwood trees planted outside its big building in New Jersey, a subtle callback to NYSE’s 1792 founding under a buttonwood tree on Wall Street. And NYSE still owns its big fancy classical temple at 11 Wall Street in lower Manhattan, and it still has human floor traders who show up to work every day to mill around on the trading floor and provide pleasing background footage for business television shows. Oh fine, fine, fine, the floor traders also trade stocks, but really the computers could do that themselves; the real purpose of the Corinthian columns and the trading floor and the traders in their jackets is mostly to create a simulacrum of a stock exchange that is legible to humans watching stock-market shows on TV. “The company touts the 30 media outlets on its trading floor, and the building’s iconic neo-classical facade, as reasons to list there.” You wouldn’t want to film a markets show from the data center in New Jersey. The computers would just hum quietly, and you’d never get them to cheer at anything you say. If this is your model of the NYSE floor—and I admit that it is exaggerated and that the floor traders actually do useful trading work—then you might want NYSE to lean into the simulacrum a bit. For instance, there are some NYSE floor traders who are famous for doing a good job of looking like floor traders, with fun hair and excitable mannerisms. Why not hire more of them, and drop the requirement that they trade stocks? Get a diverse, attractive crew of scenery-chewing actors, put them in trading jackets, and let them concentrate on running around looking excited or panicked and shouting “buy” or “sell” without having to worry about actually entering any orders. Maybe a few of them could be proficient in stage combat, and on particularly stressful trading days you could have a fake brawl break out. A few of them could be tap dancers, and on particularly boring trading days you could have a choreographed tap number break out. That would be good financial television; I would watch that. If NYSE’s floor is basically a TV set, why not focus on making exciting television rather than on efficient trading? You think I’m kidding but nope, here is surely the best market structure story of 2018: One day in late 2016, executives at the Big Board ordered dozens of regulatory staffers to head down to the trading floor so it looked busier than it really was — an elaborate ruse to impress the chief executive of Snap Inc. as he weighed whether to list the vanishing-photo app maker’s shares there, The Post has learned. NYSE brass hatched the sneaky sham, secretly caught on video by a disgusted employee, after Snap CEO Evan Spiegel remarked during a Nov. 18, 2016, tour of the exchange’s historic building at 11 Wall St. that the trading floor looked empty, according to a source. In response, Thomas Farley, then the president of the exchange, promptly ordered regulatory officials to fill it up, insiders said. (Farley denies this, and it is not at all clear if Spiegel ever saw the newly populated trading floor, though he did ultimately decide to list Snap on NYSE.) This is obviously worse than my proposal to use actors. For one thing, there is no reason to think that regulatory staffers would be particularly good at pretending to trade. “Instead of shouting, shoving and barking into phones, the officials were standing around chatting in a scene that looked more like a cocktail party,” reports the Post. Also, though, do you really want your regulatory staffers involved in this sort of, like, meta-spoofing? One thing that market regulators tend to focus on is traders who put in pretend orders or do pretend trades in order to create the misleading impression of demand for a stock. This is generally considered to be bad. “Market manipulation,” is a term that is sometimes thrown around; you’re not supposed to trick people into trading stocks by making them think, incorrectly, that a lot of people are already trading stocks. It does seem a bit much for market regulators to trick a company’s CEO into selling stock at NYSE by making him think, incorrectly, that a lot of people were trading stocks there.

My main reaction yesterday to the news that Robinhood Financial LLC, the free-stock-trading-for-millennials-on-your-phone app company, will offer a new “checking & savings” account with a 3 percent interest rate was: “Huh, interchange fees are too high.” Like the basic idea of the Robinhood account is: You give Robinhood money; They invest it in short-term Treasury securities paying, say, 2.4 percent; They pay you 3 percent. Right away you can see the problem there: The stuff that Robinhood buys with your money doesn’t pay them enough to cover the interest they pay you. “Robinhood says it will be able to make money on the service,” reports Bloomberg’s Julie Verhage, “by investing customers’ deposits into low risk products like short term Treasury bills, running a leaner business than most banks and collecting interchange fees via Mastercard on debit card transactions.” The first approach—buying securities that yield something less than 3 percent—can limit Robinhood’s losses but seems unlikely to turn a profit.[2] The second approach—“running a leaner business”—again can limit expenses, but not to a number below zero. And so you are left with interchange fees.[3] That is: You buy a sandwich with your Robinhood debit card; The sandwich shop pays a portion of the sandwich price to Mastercard as a fee for facilitating the transaction; Mastercard pays a portion of that fee to Robinhood for issuing the card; Robinhood pays a portion of that fee to you, as part of your interest. In an efficient world, the sandwich would just be cheaper, but here we are. I suppose the argument is that existing interchange fees need to cover banks’ relatively high costs of issuing credit and debit cards (and having branches, and having appropriate regulatory capital, and, to be fair, giving you money through credit-card rewards programs), while Robinhood’s lower costs mean that they don’t need the whole fee and can pass a lot of it on to you. There is a lot of confusion about what Robinhood’s thing is . Delightfully, it is called “Robinhood Checking & Savings,” apparently because calling it a “checking account” or a “savings account” would come too close to implying that it is a real bank account insured by the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., while “checking & savings” is not a thing and so does not carry that implication. A magic ampersand! “Instead,” reports Verhage, “because the product will be offered by the broker-dealer arm of the company, it will be insured by the Securities Investor Protection Corp., which covers brokerage accounts.” SIPC insures against brokerage failures but not loss in value ; if your brokerage fails you get back the stuff that was in your account, but if that stuff loses value that’s your problem. In any case SIPC was surprised to hear that it’s insuring “checking & savings” accounts now: In an email to Barron’s the head of the SIPC cast doubt on the idea that it would insure checking or savings accounts. “SIPC protects cash that is deposited with a brokerage firm for one limited purpose...the purpose of purchasing securities,” wrote Stephen P. Harbeck, the president and CEO of SIPC. “Cash deposited for other reasons would not be protected.” Harbeck told Verhage: “I disagree with the statement that these funds are protected by SIPC,” Stephen Harbeck, president and chief executive officer of SIPC, said in an interview Friday. “Had they called us, I would have told them what I just told you in that I have serious concerns about this. This has gigantic ramifications for the banking industry.” So … there … you … go … I guess? Still there is a deeper strangeness here. My Bloomberg Opinion colleague Brian Chappatta writes that this is basically just a money-market fund, which strikes me as essentially correct, but I am not at all sure that it is technically a money-market fund. Like, there is no mention of an actual fund in Robinhood’s disclosure so far, and for all we know Robinhood might invest your money directly in securities, or offer only an unsecured claim, or something else. Money-market funds are themselves sort of a regulatory arbitrage, a way to issue bank accounts without the restrictions, and the capital requirements, of actually running a bank. For that reason many people find them to be quite unsightly and systemically risky, but they have also been somewhat tamed: There are lots of restrictions on what money-market funds can do, and on how bank-account-like they can be made to seem, to try to limit their systemic risks. But in the broadest possible sense, anyone could issue bank-account-like things without actually running a bank. Like I could just take your money, and promise to give it back to you whenever you want, and pay you 3 percent interest, and invest your money in Treasury bills or corporate bonds or Bitcoins or lottery tickets or an operating business or anything else that I wanted to. If the stuff I bought paid more than 3 percent, I’d keep the excess; if it lost value, then I wouldn’t have enough money to pay you back and we’d both feel pretty bad about it. If I called this thing “Matt Bank Accounts” I might get in trouble for, in essence, impersonating a bank, but if I called it “Matt Short-Term Funding Fun Party” I might be fine. “Matt Checking & Savings,” maybe? But banks are heavily regulated, and have capital requirements, because this business model is inherently risky: Issuing demand deposits to make longer-term investments creates the risk that depositors will run and you won’t have enough money to pay them. It’s possible that not just anyone should be allowed to do it, and that moving fast and breaking things, in the area of inventing new demand-deposit products, is not the best idea.

Here is a story about the 1MDB scandal that has ensnared Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and made Lloyd Blankfein’s retirement festivities somewhat less festive: It’s enough to shock the firm’s well-connected former partners, who gathered in a hotel near the bank’s Manhattan headquarters Wednesday night for their annual dinner. Though the group tends to pooh-pooh popular criticism, many veterans are disturbed that the firm allegedly ignored or missed red flags and are annoyed by the hit to its image, according to interviews with 10 former partners, including members of the powerful management committee. To them, it’s the biggest threat to Goldman’s reputation since the firm’s post-crisis makeover. Goldman was hired to help 1MDB, a Malaysian government investment fund, raise about $6.5 billion in bond offerings. Much of that money was stolen and/or used to pay bribes, and a former Goldman partner has pleaded guilty to criminal charges for knowingly assisting the theft. And 1MDB seems to have gotten a lot of senior-level attention at Goldman—Blankfein himself apparently met with the man accused of running the scam—because of its ties to Malaysia’s then-prime minister, its connection to important Middle Eastern sovereign wealth funds, and also its comically gigantic fees: Goldman was paid some $600 million for underwriting 1MDB’s bonds, or almost 10 percent of the money it raised. Those fees are now especially awkward: Two other former top partners said the amount of money Goldman Sachs made from relatively plain bond deals should have been a bright warning to its highest executives. A third partner, who sat on the management committee, was struck that the firm was the only one competing for such a fat payday. Goldman has said some of what it earned from the deals was fair compensation for the risk it was taking. Well, I mean, technically that is true, right? Like I am a boring efficient-markets guy, and I think most risks tend to be priced. You can imagine the consideration of this deal going something like this, though not in so many words: Committee: What are the biggest risks of this deal? Deal banker: Well there’s a fairly high chance that they’re raising all this money to do crime, and if that’s true we will end up looking like villains. Committee: Hmm. Deal banker: Yes. Committee: Have you thought about how we should manage that risk? Deal banker: Yes I’ve decided that the best approach is for us to be paid just oceans of money. Committee: Ah that helps, yes. Like if a deal has a ton of interest-rate risk, you demand a lot of money to do it, so that the rewards are commensurate with the risks. If it has a ton of credit risk, you demand a lot of money to do it. If it has a ton of reputational risk, or legal risk, you … walk away, sure, right, you walk away, that is the right answer, but sometimes you just demand a lot of money to do it.

“Saudi Arabia Pumps Up Stock Market After Bad News, Including Khashoggi Murder,” is the headline here: Saudi Arabia’s government has been spending billions of dollars to quietly prop up its stock market and counter selloffs that have followed repeated political crises in recent months. According to a Wall Street Journal analysis of trading data and interviews with multiple people with direct knowledge of government intervention efforts, the Saudi government has placed huge buy orders, often in the closing minutes of negative trading days, to boost the market. Ordinarily, as part of my “everything is securities fraud” schtick, I would tell you that if the chief executive officer of a public company ordered the torture, murder and dismemberment of a prominent short seller, and that news later came out and the company’s stock price dropped, that would be not only murder but also securities fraud, because shareholders bought the stock without full disclosure of the murder. But if the news came out and the stock didn’t drop, because the CEO was pumping unlimited amounts of oil money into the market to prop up the stock price, then that is … double securities fraud, somehow? I don’t know. This isn’t quite that, but it is quite something.

Let’s say you’re in the business of researching and thinking about public companies and, in the course of that research and thinking, you conclude that a public company is doing something bad. So you decide to try to stop it, using the array of normal legal means that one can use to stop bad things. Perhaps you will sue the company for doing the bad thing. Perhaps you will write to members of Congress and ask them to pass a law stopping the company from doing the bad thing. Perhaps you will call the police, or the FBI, or the SEC or FTC or CFTC or FDA or FAA or FCC or OCC or EPA or NLRB or NHTSA, and ask them to stop the company from doing the bad thing. In all of this you will act with scrupulous honesty, presenting the facts and your conclusions in good faith and complying in all respects with the rules and norms of the judicial or political or regulatory system. If, on the basis of your research and arguments, the court/Congress/regulators/whoever agree with you, then they will stop the company from doing the bad thing; if not, you will accept their verdict and move on. That seems fine, right? Now if you are in the business of researching and thinking about public companies, the way you get paid is probably by making investment decisions about those companies’ stocks. So if you determine that a company is doing something bad, and that you might be able to stop it, you might quite naturally decide to sell the company’s stock short. You do that, then you try to stop the company, and if you are successful then its stock will go down and you will make money. You will achieve two goals, both of which you sincerely desire: You will make the world better by stopping the bad thing, and also you will make money. Is that okay? A lot of people seem to think not! When Bill Ackman sold Herbalife Nutrition Ltd. stock short and then went around telling Congress and the Federal Trade Commission and anyone else who would listen that Herbalife was a bad pyramid scheme, some people disagreed with him on the merits,[1] but other people argued that regardless of whether he was correct there was something wrong with this method, that using the political or regulatory system for profit was wrong, that just the combination of (1) shorting a company and then (2) lobbying to harm that company is itself fraudulent. Or when hedge fund manager Kyle Bass shorted the stock of pharmaceutical companies and then used a process called inter partes review to try to challenge their drug patents, claiming that the patents were invalid and that makers of cheaper generic drugs should be allowed to compete with them, some people argued not that Bass was wrong on the merits but that, in the words of Senator Bob Menendez, “such conduct can have negative consequences for targeted companies and their shareholders, and it raises concerns of market manipulation and abuse.” Obviously if a company uses invalid patents to sell expensive drugs, and those patents are invalidated and competitors start selling the drugs cheaper, that will “have negative consequences” for the company’s shareholders! That does not seem like a reason to stop people from challenging those patents. But there is also that concern that the challenge, combined with the short selling, is “market manipulation and abuse.” I do not share that concern. Of course it is fraud if you are lying about the bad thing: If you short a company’s stock and then noisily go to the FBI saying the company does lots of murder, and the stock drops, and you were just making that up, then that is fraud. Generally an outside observer won’t know if you are lying about the bad thing, and might reasonably assume that your financial interest in harming the company makes it more likely that you are lying. Relatedly, there is arguably something a bit shady about doing this without telling the regulator/court/Congress/whoever that you are short the company’s stock: As they are evaluating the evidence, including the evidence that you provide, your own financial interests might be relevant to their judgments of credibility. But these are all evidentiary issues that we can assume away to isolate the pure intuition. I think that if you (1) genuinely and reasonably think that the company is doing a bad thing, (2) short its stock, (3) go to the authorities to try to get them to stop it from doing the bad thing, and (4) fully disclose your financial interests, then that is just fine. Or perhaps the concern here is not “fraud” but “market manipulation.” You short a stock, and then you take an action to make the stock go down: Isn’t that manipulation? No, I would say, but manipulation is a fuzzy subject. My rough view is that manipulation has to involve some deception, and that taking an action to change the market can be manipulation, but taking an action to change the facts in the world is, mostly, not. It is not market manipulation for a CEO who owns stock in her company to try to increase its sales. That’s just business. Or perhaps the concern is that it is insider trading. When you short the stock, you know that you are going to sue (or whatever), and no one else does: Isn’t that insider trading? No, of course not; trading on your own intentions is always legal and couldn’t be otherwise. Alternatively, you know that the company is doing a bad thing, and no one else does: Isn’t that insider trading? I suppose it is possible—if you learned about the bad thing from the CEO in confidence, say—but in most actual cases it seems unlikely. If you think a drug company’s patent is invalid, or if you think a multilevel marketer is a pyramid scheme, that’s probably based on your analysis of public information. Here is an absolutely wild bill that was proposed this week by U.S. Senators Orrin Hatch and Thom Tillis and Representative Bill Flores, called the “Hatch-Waxman Integrity Act of 2018.” It’s about inter partes review for challenging drug patents, and it’s mostly concerned with how that review works. (Basically it seems to make IPR harder, to make life easier for big branded drug companies.) But a section of the proposed law—presumably inspired by Kyle Bass—would also amend the securities laws to make it “a manipulative or deceptive device” to short the stock of a patent owner in the 90 days before or after you challenge its patent under inter partes review. I have put the text in a footnote,[2] and if you examine it closely you will notice that it does not depend on (1) whether you are honest or dishonest, or right or wrong, about the validity of the patent, (2) whether you disclose your financial interest to the Patent and Trademark Office or anyone else, or (3) whether you have any inside information about the company. If you are absolutely certain, based on public information, that a drug company obtained its patents by the most outrageous fraud, and you short the company’s stock and fully disclose that fact and then prove to everyone’s satisfaction that in fact the patents are bogus, you go to prison for securities fraud . Your fraud consists of trying to profit from your correct belief that the patents are bogus, and from your (presumably socially valuable) effort to invalidate them. I don’t even really have an argument against this. It feels like it comes from a different world, a belief system that has nothing in common with mine. I think that “securities fraud” ought to involve dishonesty, that “market manipulation” ought to involve deceptive trading practices, and that people ought to have incentives to find out socially valuable information and to challenge invalid patents. I think that part of the value of financial markets is that they create powerful financial incentives, not just to build big good businesses, but also to stop big bad businesses, to expose frauds and challenge invalid patents and criticize harmful business models. Other people just disagree!

The way normal companies work is that, when their business is good, they tend to get bigger: They keep adding new customers and building more widgets, and the cash rolls in so they can expand their factories and buy competing or complementary businesses. When their business is bad, they tend to get smaller: Customers leave, and they have less money so they sell off assets and lay off workers. When there is a sudden crisis—a factory explodes or their widgets turn out to be poisonous—they shrink rapidly, and sometimes disappear altogether in short order. The way big banks work is different. When their business is good, they expand organically or by acquisition just like regular companies do. But when their business is bad, they … tend to expand by acquisition? And when there is a sudden crisis, they tend to expand by giant acquisition: The sudden disappearance of a major bank, regulators tend to think, would be a far-reaching disaster, and so there is a lot of pressure for strong banks to acquire weak ones or, in the case of serious systemic crises, for weak but big banks to acquire even weaker ones. Anyway: The German government is intensifying efforts to help fix Deutsche Bank AG, with officials studying ways to make it easier to merge with Commerzbank AG, people familiar with the matter said. The high-level discussions -- which have included Finance Minister Olaf Scholz and Deutsche Bank Chief Executive Officer Christian Sewing-- are looking at concrete ways the government can assist in a potential combination of the country’s two largest lenders, said the people, asking not to be identified discussing the private deliberations. The talks include potentially changing existing laws to make the steps necessary for a merger less costly, they said. If you think that it is bad for a bank to be so big and systemically important that, when it runs into trouble, the government of its home country has to step in to try to make it … bigger and more systemically important … then … that solution … also seems bad? But even if you accept that that solution is correct , that the only way to fix a huge but troubled bank is to make it bigger, then you might want to think about a countercyclical bank-bigness policy. If governments have to make big banks bigger when their business is bad, maybe governments should also try to make big banks smaller when their business is good?

s.h: We’ll build the wall, and blockchain blockchain blockchain will pay for it
s.t: Here is a Republican congressman, Warren Davidson, telling Steve Inskeep at National Public Radio about his idea for President Trump’s beloved border wall: DAVIDSON: Well, I've offered a modest compromise called Buy a Brick, Build a Wall that we introduced, which lets the American people, or whomever should choose to donate - Mexicans or otherwise - to donate to the program. INSKEEP: You mean like this highway is adopted by a certain organization? You could buy a part of the wall? DAVIDSON: Sort of. You could do with this sort of, like, crowdfunding site. Or you could even do blockchain, and you could have wall coins. But you could raise the money. And frankly, if we get it right at the Treasury, you could even accept Mexican pesos. This is normally where I’d say something like, well, if you have a trusted central authority like the U.S. government that is raising money for a centralized project like building a giant wall, then you don’t really need a blockchain. You could just keep a list. In fact, I might add, because the money here is just donated and doesn’t carry any rights, you don’t even need a list: People could give you money, and you could nod and thank them, and that would be that. You don’t need a distributed ledger, or any ledger, to keep track of people who just gave you money and don’t expect anything back. But here those criticisms seem a bit beside the point. Surely Davidson is not proposing using the blockchain to pay for the wall because he has a good understanding, or a bad understanding, of the appropriate use cases for blockchain technology. He is just saying some words. “The truth-values of his statements are of no central interest to him,” as Frankfurt says. My two takeaways here are: (1) Man, this guy gets to write laws, and (2) someone is definitely going to be selling WallCoins by this afternoon.

s.h: In a fake gold rush, sell fake shovels
s.t: I laughed at this paragraph in a story about cryptocurrency fraud AriseBank, which was founded by Jared Rice and Stanley Ford, raised about $4.25 million from investors, and was supposedly going to “set up over 1,000 ATMs that would let users tap into their cryptocurrency accounts”: Mr. Rice sent $1.3 million to a New York man as payment for a bank, according to court records. The man didn’t have a bank to sell, according to the records. The receiver is separately suing that individual in an effort to recoup money for investors. People running a crypto scam—especially one with “bank” in its name—might want to control a real bank to make the scam more convincing. But people running a crypto scam are almost uniquely unqualified to be able to tell a real bank from a fake one. This creates opportunities for derivative scams. It is an amazing and rather beautiful feature of human society that people who run scams are constantly falling for the dumbest scams themselves.

“Private markets are the new public markets,” I keep saying, as giant private tech unicorns like Uber Technologies Inc. and Lyft Inc. and Airbnb Inc. and Palantir Technologies Inc. and WeWork Cos. and Slack Technologies Inc. raise billions of dollars from investors at public-company-like valuations while becoming household names, employing lots of people, doing business around the world, and generally looking as big and important and well-funded as public companies used to be. But what if that is just an accident? It is true now, and it was true a year ago, but it might not be true next year. Uber and Lyft both confidentially filed for initial public offerings recently, and Airbnb and Palantir and WeWork and Slack are all rumored to be thinking about going public soon. Plenty of other companies have recently left the Enchanted Forest of the Unicorns for the open meadows of the public markets, and they’re basically fine. Perhaps a new generation of unicorns will grow up to replace Uber et al. Or perhaps not; the list of big unicorns in 2018 looks a lot like the list of big unicorns in 2016, except shorter. I have generally argued that the rise of unicorns is a deep feature of the economy, as it has become easier for U.S. companies to raise money privately due to more global pools of capital, more concentration of wealth in the hands of private investors, better technology to reach potential investors, etc. But it is also possible that structural choices about whether your giant multinational corporation should be public or private are essentially fashion-based. Once upon a time it was cool to ring the opening bell on the stock exchange, so founders of hot tech companies raced to go public so they could ring that bell. Now it is cool to be a unicorn—a mythical beast!—and companies stay private longer. But as the cool unicorns go public, the Enchanted Forest might start to feel less enchanted, and maybe it’ll be cool to be public again. Still it is hard for me to get all that excited about an Uber IPO. You can track Uber’s quarterly financial performance, and its stock-price fluctuations, and its activist shareholder campaigns, now! Uber is a giant public company that happens to be private; when it happens to go public, not that much will change. Here you can read my Bloomberg Opinion colleague Shira Ovide, and Axios’s Dan Primack, arguing that there’s no particular reason for Uber and Lyft to race each other to go public. “The ‘IPO window’ is a real factor for smaller or even mid-sized issuers,” writes Primack about Uber and Lyft and Slack, “but these three can go when they're ready, almost regardless of macro market conditions.” I agree, but I almost think that understates things. The “IPO window” is a thing if you think that an IPO is an important threshold, that crossing over from private to public is a risky and fraught process that might fail. If Uber wants to go public, though, it will just go public. If the stock market is bad, it might go public at a price that it doesn’t like, but why should Uber or I or anyone care about that? There are plenty of public companies whose stocks trade at prices they don’t like. Uber’s stock, quite recently, traded at a price it didn’t like. If it goes public at a price it doesn’t like, that will be a lot like remaining private at a price it doesn’t like, and if the price later goes up while it is public that will be about as good as if the price goes up before it goes public. Yes, if it goes public at a price it doesn’t like, it will raise less money for itself and its investors, but, again, it raises a lot of money in private markets now, and once it goes public it might well keep raising money, and either way it will be affected by price fluctuations. A strong stock market will be good for Uber’s stock price and a weak stock market will be bad for Uber’s stock price, but more in the way that that is true of all public companies than in the way that it is traditionally supposed to matter for IPO candidates. Meanwhile, here is a story about how Airbnb and Slack are considering doing direct listings, like Spotify Technology SA did, rather than actual IPOs. The direct listing is the purest way for a company to indicate that it doesn’t think going public is a big deal: It doesn’t raise money, doesn’t build a book of demand, doesn’t court and hand-pick its shareholders; it just flips a switch and is private one day and public the next. It’s a fitting way for unicorns to exit the Enchanted Forest. Elsewhere, Morgan Stanley seems to have beaten out Goldman Sachs Group Inc. to lead Uber’s IPO, which I certainly hope is because the lead Morgan Stanley banker moonlights as an Uber driver.

A credit default swap is basically a bet on whether a company will default on its debt. When the company defaults, people who sold CDS on that company generally have to pay money to people who bought that CDS. Generally the people who sold the CDS do not want to pay that money, while the people who bought the CDS do want them to pay that money. If the company is clever enough, this creates an opportunity. It can go to the people who sold CDS and say “if you give us some money, we will be able to avoid default, and you will not have to pay out a larger amount of money on your CDS.” And the people who sold the CDS will offer the company some money. But then it can go to the people who bought CDS and say “if you give us some money to keep our business going despite a default, we will be happy to default on our debt, and you will get paid out a larger amount of money on your CDS.” And the people who bought the CDS will offer the company some money. And then the company can just run an auction and do whatever the side that can pay more wants it to do. “Nice CDS you’ve got there, shame if someone was to [default][not default],” companies can tell each side, and then see who wants it more. There are examples. Back in 2013, Codere SA got money from CDS buyers, so it defaulted. In 2014, RadioShack Corp. got money from CDS sellers, so it did not default. (Until their CDS expired. Then it did.) These trades were a little unsatisfying, though, to me, because they seemed to be pure bilateral negotiations rather than value-maximizing auctions. I wrote at the time: Now, Codere was a lovely trade, and RadioShack is a lovely trade, but the world still awaits the Hegelian synthesis of the two. I want to see a financially distressed company with a lot of CDS outstanding run an auction to decide whether to default or not. CDS writers could offer favorable financing terms to keep the company afloat without a default. CDS buyers could offer even more favorable terms to keep the company afloat with a quick harmless Codere-style default. And then, you know, they keep bidding. They're just giving the company each other's money. Whoever wants it more will offer the best terms. Since then—and I would like to claim credit for this though that is probably unjustified—since then companies have gotten much better about doing just that. McClatchy Co., for instance, agreed to raise money on favorable terms from someone who had sold CDS on its bonds, in exchange for making those bonds essentially un-defaultable, but then ended up raising money on even more favorable terms from people who had bought that CDS, in exchange for not doing that. It heard from both sides, and made its choice. Sears Holdings Corp. has very much defaulted on its debt—it filed for bankruptcy in October—but for somewhat technical reasons it gets to play this game too. CDS on Sears will definitely pay out (it’s bankrupt), but Sears owns some weird notes from itself that will end up setting the price of that CDS: Effectively, if those notes are delivered into the CDS settlement auction, the CDS will pay out a lot and the CDS sellers will be sad, while if they are not delivered into the auction the CDS will pay out less and the CDS buyers will be sad. So Sears—or, at least, its bankruptcy estate—could do a really explicit auction: It could just put the notes up for sale, and the CDS buyers could try to buy them (and deliver them into the auction to make CDS pay out more), and the CDS sellers could try to buy them (and hold them out of the auction to make CDS pay out less), and whoever wanted it more would win, and either way Sears would get the money. It is an elegant perfection of the idea of making CDS buyers and sellers compete with each other to benefit the underlying company, though it would be even more elegant if the company wasn’t already bankrupt. And in fact Sears did that: It auctioned off those notes, and the winner was Cyrus Capital Partners, a hedge fund that is widely believed to have sold a lot of Sears CDS, which paid $82.5 million for the notes. And I rejoiced a little in this triumph of economic rationality. But I have to tell you that there are complaints. In particular, one CDS buyer, Omega Advisors Inc., has objected to the note sale, arguing in effect that it wasn’t a fair and open auction, that Sears basically gave Cyrus a sweetheart deal—selling it more notes than were supposed to be auctioned, and agreeing not to sell any more—and could have gotten more money by running a fairer auction. It is hard as an outsider for me to evaluate these claims—perhaps Sears made a rational choice about how it could maximize value, perhaps not—but they seem plausible, and they make me sad. If you’re going to run an auction to squeeze money out of your CDS buyers and sellers, please, do it properly, and squeeze as much money as possible. That is the main lesson that I take from all of this, but I might be weird. Here is former Commodity Futures Trading Commission member Bart Chilton’s take, with the headline “Sears’ Death Gives Life To Crisis-Era Derivatives Demons,” and with dire warnings that Cyrus is involved in “potential CDS market manipulation,” that “many traditional creditors and investors may no longer feel comfortable lending to companies—even healthy ones—now that the reliability of the CDS market is compromised,” and that strong action is needed “to expel the malignancies festering in this multi-trillion-dollar market.” (Here is the pleasingly peevish response from the International Swaps and Derivatives Association.) I will admit that my model of CDS squeezing—that if a company is in or near default, it should go to its CDS buyers and sellers and try to extract as much money as possible out of them—is a much better model ex post than it is ex ante. If a near-default company can just call up some derivatives traders with whom it has never had any direct dealings and get them to give it free money, then that feels a lot like a windfall. But it probably is good for companies in general if CDS buyers and sellers think of CDS as mostly a bet on the creditworthiness of a company, and not as a tool for the company to arbitrarily extract value out of derivatives traders if it gets near to default. The more joyfully weird the CDS market is for companies near default, the less useful it will be the rest of the time.

If I start a company, and raise money from investors, and use that money to buy a widget factory and produce widgets, then my company is what you’d normally call a “company.” If I raise that money in a public offering, my company is a “public company,” and if it’s big enough it will get into stock-market indexes, and mutual funds will buy shares, and it will be part of the normal system of normal public companies. If I start a company, and raise money from investors, and use that money to buy shares or bonds of other companies that manufacture widgets and sprockets and whatsits, then my company is, to a reasonable approximation, what you’d normally call a “mutual fund.” You could call it a company—it is a company, and securities law calls it an “investment company”—but you mostly wouldn’t; you’d call it a mutual fund. (You might call it an exchange-traded fund, or a private-equity fund, or whatever, depending on the specifics.) And it wouldn’t get to do a lot of public company things. It wouldn’t be in any stock-market indexes, and other mutual funds would generally not buy its shares. In fact, Securities and Exchange Commission rules discourage mutual funds from buying other mutual funds, by requiring them to disclose the expenses of the funds they buy as part of their own expense ratios: If a mutual fund buys shares in another mutual fund, it counts that other fund’s management expenses in its own disclosures to customers (whereas if it buys shares in a regular company , that company’s management costs are not treated as mutual-fund costs). But most mutual funds mostly wouldn’t buy shares in other mutual funds anyway. It just seems sort of lazy, you know? If I start a company, and raise money from investors, and use that money to make loans to widget manufacturers, though, what is my company? It might be a “bank.” A bank is, for these purposes, mostly a company: Banks get into stock-market indexes, mutual funds invest in them, etc. Or it might be a finance company or a peer-to-peer lender or something that is also a company. Or it might be a “business development company.” A BDC, despite the C, seems to not be a company: It is more like a mutual fund that buys loans than a company that does a business. But that is a vague and slippery distinction. The BDC is sourcing loans, making credit decisions, negotiating terms, extending credit; are those actions more business-y actions like a bank does or investment-y actions like a mutual fund does? Anyway the SEC comes down on the mutual-fund side: Due to the SEC rules, if mutual funds buy [BDC] stock, they have to include BDC operating expenses in the expense ratios that funds must calculate and disclose to prospective investors. Because that would force mutual funds to overstate their costs, the BDC industry says most funds shun their shares. Adding to frustrations is that the SEC regulations have a similar impact on the expense ratios of broad equity indexes like those operated by Standard & Poor’s and Russell. So indexes exclude BDCs, further restricting investment because many mutual funds and exchange traded funds are specifically set up to track benchmarks. That’s from a Bloomberg News story about how BDCs are lobbying to try to change those rules, which they say are “misleading and materially overstate” expenses. The story casts this as essentially a political-power story (will lobbyists for powerful firms get what they want?), and the lobbyists cast it as essentially a truth-for-investors story (do the SEC rules create accurate disclosure?), but to me it seems like a philosophical story about what counts as a company and what counts as an investment fund. Also about who decides. We talk a lot around here about the power of index creators: Many investors just want to buy “the market,” as approximated by some index, and so the index creators have a lot of power to make decisions about what sorts of companies count as part of “the market.” Sometimes these decisions are about salient controversial issues, like whether dual-class shares should be allowed or cast out into darkness. But sometimes they are about weird subtleties that you’d barely even think of as decisions. Of course “the market” is limited to public companies, not private ones, even if big mutual funds have some ability to buy shares in private companies. And of course ”the market” is limited to companies, not investment funds; having an index that included investment funds would be absurd and recursive. (You can’t very well make an index fund track an index that includes index funds, can you?) But you still have to decide which is which.

The most basic investing scam is: I convince you to invest your money with me. I steal it. It’s a good scam (for me) in that it is efficient: All of the money that you invest, I steal, which maximizes my chances of buying a yacht and sailing away from the criminal authorities. The margins are good. On the other hand there are some limits to how big this scam can get. I can send you fake account statements, etc., to try to persuade you that your money is well invested and you should give me more, but eventually if I want to raise a lot of money I will have to spend some of it on creating verisimilitude rather than steal it all for myself. The Ponzi scheme is a key refinement, in which the verisimilitude is created by using some of the money to give other investors actual “investing” returns. (Actual returns, but not actually from investing.) The scam is: I convince you to invest your money with me. I steal some of it. I convince someone else to invest their money with me. I give some of it back to you as “investing returns,” and steal the rest. Etc. This has much lower margins than the simple scam, since I am giving so much of the money back to investors instead of stealing it for myself, but the advantage is that this scam can grow much bigger and operate much longer. In the limit case, if you run a really really big Ponzi for a really really long time, you will end up stealing almost none of the money. On a percentage basis, I mean. If you run a really big Ponzi then stealing only a tiny bit of the money can still buy you some very nice yachts. So, paradoxically, a really big Ponzi is, for the victims, relatively good: Most of the money wasn’t really stolen, and can maybe be recovered! For instance: A decade after Bernard Madoff was arrested for running the world’s biggest Ponzi scheme, the bitter fight to recoup investors’ lost billions has astounded experts and victims alike. While no one will ever collect the phantom profits Madoff pretended he was earning, the cash deposits by his clients have been the primary objective for Irving Picard, a New York lawyer overseeing liquidation of Madoff’s firm in bankruptcy court. So far he’s recovered $13.3 billion—about 70 percent of approved claims—by suing those who profited from the scheme, knowingly or not. And Picard has billions more in his sights. “That kind of recovery is extraordinary and atypical,” said Kathy Bazoian Phelps, a bankruptcy lawyer at Diamond McCarthy LLP in Los Angeles who isn’t involved in the case. Recoveries in Ponzi schemes range from 5 percent to 30 percent, and many victims don’t get anything, Phelps said. Yeah but that is just Ponzi economies of scale. The bigger the Ponzi, the better the chances of recovery; you just can’t spend $13 billion on cocaine. Obviously this is a bit rough on some of the people who innocently invested in Madoff’s Ponzi, got back a nice but not earth-shattering return for many years, spent the money, and are now getting it clawed back, but still it’s better than everyone losing everything. Today is the 10-year anniversary of Bernie Madoff’s arrest, which is a little mind-blowing since we were just commemorating the 10-year anniversary of the Lehman bankruptcy a few months ago. It is somehow weird that Madoff and the global financial crisis live on the same timeline. Lehman’s failure was a crucial moment in a crisis that still reverberates today. Madoff’s failure, huge and shocking as it was at the time, feels like an odd curiosity these days. They even got most of the money back! In any case, here is a roundup of “How Madoff's Multi-Billion Fraud Changed the Hedge Fund Industry.” And here is a story about how Madoff’s scheme created the modern SEC whistle-blower industry, which can seem a little bit like its own form of grift. “Two individuals filed so many frivolous reward requests—one person has filed 143—that they were banned from making future requests, according to agency records.” If you start a program to give multi-million-dollar rewards to people who know about fraud, it is going to attract some fraud. Are Tesla Inc. and Elon Musk complying with the terms of their settlement with the Securities and Exchange Commission? No, the answer is no, not at all, but to be fair they have a good reason, which is that Elon Musk does not respect the SEC, as he made clear on “60 Minutes” this weekend: Lesley Stahl: Look at you. Elon Musk: I want to be clear. I do not respect the SEC. I do not respect them. I am not an expert in, like, journalism, but it does seem to me that “look at you” might be the best possible interview question to ask Elon Musk. If Musk is up for it I will happily interview him for Bloomberg and I promise that my questions will consist solely of saying “look at you” repeatedly; I bet it will break a lot of news. Anyway here is the lead-up to that exchange, and I write a lot of jokey hypothetical dialogue in this newsletter, some of it involving Elon Musk, so I want to emphasize that this is real dialogue taken directly from CBS News’s transcript: Lesley Stahl: Have you had any of your tweets censored since the settlement? Elon Musk: No. Lesley Stahl: None? Does someone have to read them before they go out? Elon Musk: No. Lesley Stahl: So your tweets are not supervised? Elon Musk: The only tweets that would have to be say reviewed would be if a tweet had a probability of causing a movement in the stock. Lesley Stahl: And that's it? Elon Musk: Yeah, I mean otherwise it's, "Hello, First Amendment." Like Freedom of Speech is fundamental. Lesley Stahl: But how do they know if it's going to move the market if they're not reading all of them before you send them? Elon Musk: Well, I guess we might make some mistakes. Who knows? Lesley Stahl: Are you serious? Elon Musk: Nobody's perfect. Okay really all of the questions here are pretty great. “Are you serious,” for instance, is almost as good a question as “look at you.” But also: If you’ve agreed with the SEC—as Tesla definitely, definitely, definitely, 100 percent, in a settlement approved by a federal judge, has[1]—to have a securities lawyer review Musk’s tweets and pre-approve them if they might move the stock price, then, right, “how do they know if it’s going to move the market if they’re not reading all of them before you send them?” One could imagine a different CEO giving a different answer: “I do personal tweets myself but run anything about the business by the lawyers, and err on the side of caution,” say, or “I like to think that after years of service as a public-company CEO I know what is and isn’t material to the stock price.” Musk did not give those answers! It’s super weird. Tesla agreed to get its Musk-tweet-reviewing house in order within 90 days after the settlement; they still have a month or so, so this isn’t technically a violation. Perhaps after that deadline Musk will give different answers ha ha ha ha no come on there’s no chance whatsoever that that will happen. Who would make it happen? The securities lawyers in charge of implementing Tesla’s SEC settlement will come to Musk—if they haven’t already—and say “you need to run your tweets by us before you send them,” and he will say “says who,” and they will say “says this settlement with the SEC that we signed and that a judge approved,” and he will say “Hello, First Amendment,” and they will say “well that is not really how this works,”[2] and he will turn his back on them and go back to tweeting about pedos and Mars and short sellers and how much he hates the SEC, and they will wander away looking sad and nervous. We really live in a golden age for legal realism. It used to be that “because it is against the law,” or “because we have agreed not to,” was widely accepted as a sufficient reason not to do something. Obviously there were murders and financial crimes and so forth, but, like, when corporate CEOs went on television they were careful to say things like “we follow the law and abide by our commitments and respect our regulators.” Now—and I am not thinking solely about Musk—a much stronger sense of “well who will make me” has crept into legal analysis. Oh sure Musk will ignore his SEC settlement, but what is the SEC going to do about it? Sue him again? I mean, maybe, right? The thing is that he hasn’t really done anything bad ; he has tweeted mean stuff about the SEC, and sort of joked that he was stepping down as Tesla’s CEO, but there’s not much here to really alarm or deceive shareholders. If the SEC didn’t have a settlement with Tesla requiring him to knock off the impulsive tweeting, it wouldn’t have any real complaints about Musk’s recent tweets, and just having the settlement is not necessarily a good reason for it to intervene. Having the settlement and watching Musk go on television to say that he doesn’t respect the SEC—while the SEC and Justice Department are also looking into Tesla’s disclosures about its production targets—might be another story.

A trend in recent years has been for famous founders of big important hedge funds to kick out their outside investors and remake their funds as family offices. There are various possible reasons for this—popular ones include performance being too good, performance being too bad, legal troubles, and just getting older and tired of dealing with investors—but they all tend to end up with the famous manager running a multi-billion-dollar investment pool consisting mainly of his own (and his employees’) money. Och-Ziff Capital Management Group LLC went the other way last week: Billionaire Dan Och is pulling the majority of his capital from his namesake company as he prepares the company for his retirement early next year. The hedge fund manager said in a statement Thursday that he is redeeming all of his liquid fund investments at Och-Ziff Capital Management Group LLC, which announced a series of other changes at the publicly-traded hedge fund firm. The other changes are designed both to shore up the firm’s finances—including a reverse stock split to avoid delisting—and to transfer power and ownership to Och’s successors, including CEO Robert Shafir. “I look forward to moving on based on my confidence that Oz will be in good hands with Rob and his leadership team,” says Och in the press release, but that confidence does not seem to extend to keeping his money in the funds? His money was only about 3 percent of assets under management anyway. Arguably this is a better model of hedge-fund transition. The standard model seems to tie the life cycle of a hedge fund to the life cycle of its manager: As a brash young up-and-comer, he starts a small fund that makes bold moves and achieves stellar performance; on the back of that success he raises lots of money and institutionalizes his firm and settles down in middle age to collect a lot of fees with modest returns; as he gets old and rich he decides he doesn’t need the hassle of clients and retires to a family office; and then, presumably—there is less precedent for this so far—he dies and his fortune goes to heirs and charity and perhaps a boringly managed foundation. This is a very nice life cycle, if you are that hedge fund manager, but it is perhaps less satisfactory for the other people involved. (Except the heirs.) There’s a lot of value in a perpetual corporate entity! Clients and employees might feel more secure if their long-term relationship is with an institutional entity rather than a rich guy who might close the fund on a whim. And certainly if you go public and raise outside money—as most hedge fund firms don’t, but as Och-Ziff did—then you are sort of committing to perpetuity. A perpetual hedge-fund firm ought to survive, not only its founder’s retirement , but even the withdrawal of his money . There is something healthy—and I don’t want to exaggerate this; after all Och-Ziff is also fighting not to get delisted—but in the abstract there is something healthy about a hedge-fund firm whose founder decides to withdraw most of his money and that mentions that in the third page of the press release. Meh, he’s just one investor. In other hedge fund news, “AQR Capital Management’s flagship risk parity mutual fund, which has suffered big outflows, will no longer be billed as a risk parity fund.”

s.h: People are worried about bond market liquidity
s.t: The staff of the Bank of Canada are worried enough about liquidity in the market for Canadian government bonds that they published this neat discussion paper proposing “four blue-sky ideas for lowering the cost of funding the Government of Canada’s debt without increasing its risk profile” by increasing liquidity. Two of these ideas involve open-market operations (“to reopen the issuance of scarce bonds,” or “to conduct more switch operations (exchanges of less liquid GoC securities for new, more liquid bonds).” The other two are about reducing the number of bonds Canada sells in order to improve liquidity in each bond: Specifically, the third idea is to eliminate coupon payments from government debt and issue debt on a simpler and fixed maturity schedule. Issuing zero-coupon debt would eliminate a key difference between GoC securities and increase their fungibility. Combined with a fixed maturity schedule, it would simplify the issuance of GoC securities throughout their life cycles and increase their liquidity. Our fourth and most radical idea is to push defragmentation to its logical end. We describe a government debt program centred around three perpetuities—one to replace bonds, one to replace bills and one to replace Real Return Bonds. The perpetuities would be standardized, streamlined and issued in greater size than the most liquid bonds available anywhere today. These features would make them extremely liquid on the secondary market, which would in turn decrease their cost at issuance. You sometimes see similar proposals in the world of corporate bonds: Each company just has too many bonds, and they are not interchangeable with each other, and so each is less liquid than they’d be if they were all somehow combined. There is only so far corporates can go with that, but with hypothetical staff discussion papers for large rich own-currency sovereign issuers the sky is the limit. The fourth idea here is for Canada to issue three perpetual bonds: one with a fixed rate (and a price that varies with prevailing interest rates), one with a floating rate “set at the central bank’s monetary policy target rate and paid frequently, such as monthly (or even daily)” (and, one assumes, a fairly stable price), and one with an inflation-linked rate. If the government has a surplus it can buy back bonds on the open market; if it has a deficit it can issue new perpetuities (totally fungible with the existing ones) at the market price; if it wants to change its interest-rate profile it can buy back some fixed-rate (long-duration) bonds and sell some floating-rate (short-duration) ones, or vice versa. I am fond of this idea purely as an aesthetic matter. For one thing, there is something pleasingly counterintuitive about saying that a government can get any mix of debt maturities that it likes with just two types of bonds,[3] both of them perpetual . A perpetual floating-rate bond is effectively a very short-term bond, a perpetual fixed-rate bond is effectively a very long-term bond, and you can get any average duration you like by combining the two. For another thing, perpetuities are neat because they undercut a lot of boring political arguments. “We can’t keep borrowing like this forever,” say politicians; “if we take on debt, it will need to be repaid.” In fact, rich countries like the United States have more or less been borrowing like this forever, and just paying off that debt and living debt-free seems both impossible and undesirable. (For one thing, the money could be used for better things; for another, people like owning government bonds.) But as long as governments are issuing term debt, two- or five- or 30-year bonds, the maturities of the bonds do create the impression that they need to be repaid. (And they do, though normally just by issuing new bonds.) Issuing only perpetuities removes that illusion and reveals the debt for what it is, a structural feature of the economy rather than a short-term IOU that the government needs a plan to pay back. Also if you only issue perpetuities, there will be people who want something other than perpetuities, and how will they get it? Yes that’s right it’s financial engineering! Intermediaries would have a new role serving investors who desire payments with some maturity, duration or timing. Intermediaries can replicate any cash-flow structure desired by holding an appropriate portfolio of perpetuities or perpetuity derivatives and rebalancing it occasionally. As some clients are unable to do this or would find it too costly, intermediaries could repackage the fixed payments of perpetuities to meet the demand of clienteles. We see a competitive system of intermediaries who are paid to serve clients as a better way to address clienteles. Asset-backed securities of Canadian government debt! It’s financial engineering without the (well, without much) risk, letting financial engineers exercise their talents and have some fun without much chance of crashing the financial system.

Yesterday I went to a Federal Trade Commission hearing about “concerns that acquisitions and holdings of non-controlling ownership interests in competing companies, for example by institutional investors, may have anticompetitive effects.” And both on Twitter and in person during breaks at the hearing, people would come up to me and ask “so are index funds illegal yet or what?” So I feel like my schtick is working. You know all this stuff, right? There are worries that common ownership of multiple companies in the same industry by big institutional investors will lessen competition among those companies. That worry, in its modern form, comes from a paper by José Azar, Martin Schmalz and Isabel Tecu, which claims to find that common ownership of U.S. airlines by big investors has led to increased prices and reduced competition. Other empirical and theoretical papers about other industries have followed. I have been writing about it since 2015, and I’ve enjoyed phrasing the question maximally as “should index funds be illegal?” That is a little bit of a joke, but not really, because if you take this stuff seriously enough then it does seem like large diversified shareholders—index funds but also other mutual funds—would pose a problem under the antitrust laws, and you’d have to do something about them. One thing I should say about this theory is that, as far as I can tell, almost no one who works in the capital markets or corporate America takes it seriously. That doesn’t mean it’s not serious—it gets a lot of attention from academics, for one thing, but it also gets increasing amounts of attention from regulators —but it is sort of an interesting empirical fact. Yesterday’s hearing featured a panel in which representatives of BlackRock Inc., the Council of Institutional Investors, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and the AFL-CIO all agreed that common ownership is not a problem and that nothing should be done about it. The Chamber of Commerce, the CII and the AFL-CIO do not, as far as I know, agree on a whole lot. But on this they are unanimous, and sort of incredulous: You called us to a hearing to talk about this? Still I continue to appreciate this theory, aesthetically but also as a matter of first principles. It seems to me that to believe the theory you only really need to believe these premises: Most managers are responsive to shareholders’ interests and want to maximize the shareholders’ wealth.[1] Most shareholders are broadly diversified and want to maximize their wealth across all companies in an industry, and really all public companies. The joint interests of all companies in an industry (as opposed to the interests of one company competing in the industry), or of all public companies together, can sometimes conflict with the interests of consumers. These premises all seem, not just reasonable, but like basic textbook stuff. Premise 1—that managers should be accountable to shareholders—is the central idea of corporate governance. Premise 2—that investors should be broadly diversified—is the central idea of modern portfolio theory. Premise 3—that the best interests of all the companies in an industry can diverge from the best interests of consumers—is the central idea of antitrust. More than that, Premises 1 and 2 are, in a sense, new : The last few decades have seen parallel movements to improve corporate governance and increase management accountability to shareholders, on the one hand, and to provide efficient low-cost diversification to investors, on the other hand. You would expect that the combined result of those two movements would be that companies would be more responsive to the interests of diversified shareholders. If those shareholders are interested in higher corporate profits generally, you might expect to see a decline in fierce competition among companies and a rise in corporate profits as companies fight less for market share. You might also see a decline in fierce competition for workers, as companies try to improve margins by keeping wages down and not trying to hire each others’ workers. One thing that seems to bother people about this argument is that Premises 1 and 2 are good . We want managers to be more responsive to shareholders—it’s called “good governance”—and we want middle-class investors to have more access to low-cost high-quality diversified investment opportunities. It is troubling to think that good governance and sensible diversification could also be bad for consumers or workers. Still it doesn’t seem crazy? The idea that the interests of capital , as a class, could differ from the interests of consumers , and that innovations (index funds, good governance) that improve the lot of capital could worsen the lot of consumers and workers, is really quite traditional. Marx would not have found it surprising!

Eddie Lampert took over Sears in 2004, through his hedge fund ESL Investments Inc. Since then he has put money into Sears Holdings Corp., and taken money out; he has made loans and done spinoffs and generally created a lot of cash flows in all directions. Also Sears filed for bankruptcy in October. The result of all of this is that the question “Has Eddie Lampert made money on Sears, or lost money, or what?” does not have a simple answer: Sure he bought Sears when its stock was worth billions of dollars and now its stock is worth no dollars, but you have to parse through a lot of details of how he put money in and what he got in return to figure out if, on balance, he’s up or down. At Institutional Investor, Michelle Celarier does some parsing and concludes that he’s up: Although current Sears shareholders have lost almost their entire investment, tens of thousands of employees have lost their jobs, and creditors — including the U.S. government — and others are owed $11 billion, Lampert has still made nearly $1.4 billion to date from his Sears investment, a number that has never been calculated before. It’s also a sum that could change radically — up or down — depending on the outcome of what is likely to be a contentious bankruptcy process, which is now unfolding. I would still like a simple (well, long) table of sources and uses, but it’s good to have a number. I want to point out one thing about Celarier’s math, though, which is that she counts not just Lampert’s and ESL’s cash flows on Sears’s stocks and bonds and loans and spinoffs and things, but also Lampert’s fees from running ESL. Here are her numbers: At its peak in early 2007, Sears had a market capitalization of nearly $30 billion — almost twice that of Amazon at the time. The stock now trades at 33 cents per share, but financial engineering — dividends, interest payments, and asset spin-offs deployed to keep the company out of bankruptcy — looks to have narrowed Lampert’s losses on an approximate $1.5 billion equity investment to close to $624 million. Those losses, however, pale in comparison to the profits Lampert made, thanks to the compensation structure of his hedge fund, which he launched in 1988 at the age of 25. At Sears’ peak, the fund owned about half of the retailer. Performance fees that ESL’s investors paid Lampert on his Sears and Kmart investments as those shares took off, amounting to almost $11 billion at the end of 2006, come to an estimated $2 billion. Now of course this is perfectly fair: If the question you are asking is “how did Eddie Lampert do on his Sears investment,” you should count up all of the cash flows to him personally; performance fees on that investment are cash flows to him, and they count. It is a different question from “how did Eddie Lampert’s hedge fund do on his Sears investment?” There the answer might well still be positive—Celarier calculates a $624 million loss on the equity but also notes that ESL still owns $2.6 billion of Sears debt, much of it secured, which will presumably have some recovery—but it’s a closer question, and it is, in any case, less positive. That latter question—how did ESL do on Sears—is the question you would want to answer if you were evaluating Lampert’s skill as an investor. Lampert made a bet on Sears, and then made a series of additional decisions about how to structure and risk-manage and monetize and double down on that bet, and the resulting series of cash flows to his investing entity is the payoff of those decisions. The ultimate division of those cash flows among the owners of that entity is irrelevant to the question of how good the investing decisions were.[2] If you are an asset allocator deciding what hedge funds to invest in, or just an investing fan deciding what great investors to admire, you’d be interested in the quality of the investment decision, measured by the cash flows to his fund. But the former question—how did Lampert himself do on Sears—might be the question you’d want to answer if you were evaluating Lampert’s skill as a hedge fund manager . Lampert made a series of decisions about Sears, and about the structure of his hedge fund, and about the marketing of that hedge fund, and the resulting series of cash flows to him is his payoff from those decisions. The ultimate source of those cash flows—from Sears, or from his hedge fund’s investors—is irrelevant to the question of, you know, whether he has a yacht.[3] I often say around here that the principal skill of a hedge fund manager is not making investments but rather continuing to manage a lucrative hedge fund . The former helps with the latter, but it is not an absolute requirement. In general assets are sensitive to performance, and fees are based on performance, so it is rare and difficult to be a purely extractive hedge fund manager over the long run. You can’t normally invest your clients’ money in a company that goes to zero and loses billions for them but still somehow makes billions of dollars for you . But it does seem tantalizingly possible, and sort of perversely impressive. Oh elsewhere Lampert and ESL are trying to buy Sears out of bankruptcy, so the sources and uses table might be forever incomplete: Mr. Lampert’s hedge fund ESL Investments Inc. is proposing to buy Sears, its real estate and brands like Kenmore in a deal that wouldn’t rely heavily on cash, and would instead use new borrowings, forgive Sears’s existing debts and roll over the company’s other debts. In a securities filing Thursday, ESL said the deal was valued at $4.6 billion, mostly from $950 million in new loans, the forgiveness of $1.8 billion in debt and $1.1 billion of assumed liabilities.

“There’s a hot new asset class where growth may be outpacing every established market,” writes Mary Childs at Barron’s: “proximity to celebrity billionaires. For charity!” We have talked about this market before, in embarrassingly self-referential ways: Childs wrote about a charity auction for lunch with Bill Ackman, and I put a joking multiples-based valuation of $54,000 on that lunch, and then a guy went and paid that price because of my valuation, and they had lunch, and Childs wrote about it again, and I wrote about it again, and I put a not-at-all-joking and entirely well-supported valuation of $2 million on lunch with me, and as of this writing no one has given me $2 million to have lunch with me but give it time, give it time. But people do seem to be spending a lot of money to hang out with famous people. Childs has some relative-value analysis of spending time with Mark Cuban and Tim Draper and Mindy Grossman, and if you are looking for lunch valuation analysis you should head over to Barron’s; I have gotten out of the lunch-investment-advice business. Still we should talk a little about the financialization of lunch. Here is Childs: This is another example of the commodification of influence. Where previously people enjoyed access through old-boy networks, country clubs, and invitation-only charity galas, like so many things it is increasingly just available for purchase, another frontier for financialization. In some ways, it’s a democratization. And, in an increasingly bifurcated economy, where a splash of fame can make a career, people are willing to pay up. Meanwhile at New York Magazine, Max Read writes about how “former Green Bay Packers quarterback Brett Favre and the rapper Soulja Boy were tricked by a group of white nationalists into recording anti-Semitic videos.” Basically Favre and others use Cameo, an app “where users can pay to have celebrities record a personalized message for them.” The celebrities can only devote so much time to doing due diligence on the coded nuance of the personalized messages, and so they suffer the fate of everything on the internet: “The white supremacists who paid Favre for the video ‘hacked’ the Brett Favre platform just as racist trolls ‘hack’ Twitter or Facebook, taking advantage of his desire to make a buck and his inability to keep track of mutating memes.” But there’s a more general economic analysis: Cameo, if it’s not obvious, is a platform, in this case not for connecting widget buyers with widget sellers, but for connecting “people who want to see famous people do things” with “people who have fame.” “Fame” is an asset that Brett Favre owns 24 hours a day, the way an Airbnb host might own her apartment. But like that Airbnb host, who leaves her apartment empty when she’s gone for the weekend, Favre isn’t wringing every last cent out of his asset — there are many hours where he’s just sitting around being famous all by himself. Cameo puts this otherwise nonproductive fame to use, by connecting him with willing buyers. It is so modern, so efficient. Sometimes Favre is famous but not using his fame; other times—when he runs into a fan at the grocery store or whatever—he is using his fame without monetizing it. An internet platform can allow him to capture more of that value. In the long run, perhaps, the result will be to internalize all externalities, eliminate all inefficiencies and all serendipity: If you get the tiniest amount of joy out of Brett Favre, or anyone, or anything, you pay for it. Anyway, I personally seem to have a very small amount of fame that I perhaps do not monetize efficiently; I should sell the right to stand next to me while I type for like $5 an hour.

Let’s say you are throwing an event, a party or a sports game or something. There is a venue, and you control access to the venue, by putting a guard at the door. You want people to come to the venue, but you want to control who can come. For instance you might want to only let in the people you invite. Or you might want to sell tickets, but you don’t want people to be able to resell those tickets without your permission. There are obviously bad ways to do this: If you just print some tickets saying “admit one,” and you sell them, then people can transfer them or perhaps even forge them, and you will not be able to tell, just from looking at the tickets, who bought tickets from you and who bought them illicitly. There are better ways to do it. For instance, you can keep a list, and sell spots on that list: People give you money, and you put them on the list. When they arrive at your venue, they identify themselves and you let them in if they’re on the list and you don’t if they’re not. If they want to resell their spots, maybe you can let them do it through your website; you could set up a ticket exchange and cap prices or take a cut of the sale price or whatever. Or if you don’t want any reselling at all you could just forbid it. The point is that you control the list. You control the venue. You sell the “tickets” (the spots on the list). You are the central controlling administrator of the event—the party, the sports game, whatever—and so it is natural for you to keep the list of who can come, and to check people off against that list. You’d have to make choices about how people would identify themselves when they buy the tickets and again when they get to the venue. They could just say “Hi I am so-and-so” and give you their driver’s license and you’d check their name against the list. Or you could give them an app that displays a QR code on their phone (and that stops working if they are taken off the list). Or whatever; you want to pair spots on the list with identities , so that only the people who have met your approval to be on the list are allowed in. Now of course if you are a party-thrower or sports team, perhaps you are not well equipped technologically to control lists. Perhaps you don’t have a nice website that allows people to resell their tickets, or you don’t understand QR codes. Perhaps there is a market opportunity for some service provider who would control your list for you, who would do the work of selling tickets (spots on the list), administering resales, etc. This service provider would control the list on your behalf, would follow your parameters on who is allowed to resell spots and how, and would, on the day of the event, give you a useful list of the people who are allowed in so you could check them off against the list. I feel incredibly stupid typing all of this but: A London stock market minnow is teaming up with a heavyweight soccer executive to use blockchain to tackle ticket scalpers. TechFinancials Inc. has signed binding terms for the new venture with Footies Tech Ltd. -- founded by Ian Ayre, former chief executive of Premier League team Liverpool Football Club -- according to a statement Thursday. The new company will help sports organizations “take full control” over ticketing, including secondary market trading configuration and enforcement, Cyprus-based TechFinancials said. THAT IS A LIST. JUST USE A DATABASE. You don’t need a trustless decentralized distributed ledger to “take full control” over ticketing. You use a blockchain when you don’t want one party to have full control over the ledger. If one party has full control over the ledger, that is just a list.
